source.title: When Structured Sparse Autoencoders Learn Consistent Concepts Across Modalities
source.authors: Wei-Duo Liao; Yunqiao Yang; Ying Wei

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It compares vanilla and structured SAE training using feature-level monosemanticity and semantic-alignment measures. This is a different operationalization from measuring native neuron responses, but it tests whether regularization changes polysemanticity-related outcomes.
record.gate_note: The study tests SAE features learned from one VLM, not the base model's individual neurons or the cited InceptionV1 neuron. It therefore bears on V5, but does not test V1–V4, V6, or V7 as stated. Results cited from prior work are not included. The paper's examples and tables include results for SAE features; the prompts in the appendix are instructions for the study's interpretation models, not instructions addressed to an AI reading or reviewing this paper.
record.test_reason: The study cites neuron polysemanticity (Olah et al. 2020) only as motivation. It trains sparse autoencoders on Qwen2.5-VL-7B residual streams and compares its own structured SAE (S²AE) with a vanilla Top-K SAE. All results are on SAE dictionary features, not on the model's own neurons. The regularizers change the SAE objective, not the model's architecture, activation function or training, so no result shows how often or how strongly the network's neurons are polysemantic. Every row is the study's own method compared against a baseline. The record's V5 link mistakes SAE training regularization for model regularization.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, but it should be stated that every claim concerns learned SAE dictionary features, not the VLM's neurons. The authors also conclude that their hierarchical VLM-then-LLM interpretation pipeline is far more reliable than direct VLM summarization (identification rate 98.8% vs 66.4% at layer 5).
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains a Top-K SAE with attention- and spatially defined visual groups plus exclusive- and group-sparsity regularizers. It measures SAE feature scores, not the original native-neuron response examples or measurement method.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary by layer, feature modality subset, and regularizer combination. The paper also reports that clustering choices (attention and spatial information) affect cluster quality, but does not report those clustering results as polysemanticity outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding exclusive and group sparsity over attention/spatial patch clusters to Top-K SAE training on Qwen2.5-VL-7B raises SAE-feature mask/cluster mIoU (layer 15: 0.516 to 0.594). It also raises multimodal-feature vision and language MS at all four layers, while EV stays above 0.99. Vision-only MS falls at layers 10–20, and the composition of feature subsets shifts a lot.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Residual polysemanticity of SAE dictionary features in VLMs can be reduced by structured sparsity regularizers in SAE training without losing reconstruction fidelity.

fits_no_version.finding: For vanilla SAE features, vision MS (about 0.49–0.51) is well below language MS (about 0.86–0.87) at every layer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features in VLMs are less monosemantic on the vision side than on the language side.

record.problems: Only one VLM is evaluated. The results concern learned SAE features rather than the base model's individual neurons. The visual alignment target is derived from the model's attention and spatial clustering, and the MS and cross-modal-consistency results depend on an automated interpretation/scoring pipeline. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the central comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported numerical results on raw native-neuron responses. Figure 8 gives example IoU values but the displayed cases do not provide a systematic result beyond the layer-5 comparison summarized in text; exact Figure 5 layer-wise values are figure-only, recorded together in r22 because the text reports a consistent improvement across layers.

untested.parts: Native neurons in image classifiers; no neuron-level analysis of the base model.
Share of polysemantic MLP neurons in language models and how it varies by layer.
Superposition as the cause of polysemanticity.
Effect of model activation function, architecture or regularization on native-neuron polysemanticity. Only the SAE's training objective is varied.
Dependence of the polysemantic classification on activation range or explanation scoring for neurons.

record.verdict_notes: Native neuron polysemanticity is cited only as motivation, and the paper calls SAE latents 'neurons', which may have misled the reader. The visual alignment targets are clusters derived from the model's own attention, and the vision reference samples are chosen partly by IoU with those clusters, so the alignment metrics partly favour the method. MS comparisons by subset are made over feature sets whose sizes change sharply between arms. No uncertainty estimates are given, and only one model is tested.

versions.untested_parts: Native neurons in image classifiers and their responses to multiple unrelated inputs, including the cited InceptionV1 example.
Polysemanticity of MLP neurons in transformer language models and its variation across layers.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by representing more sparse features than there are neurons.
Polysemanticity caused by initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.

The study varies structured regularization of SAE features in one VLM; it does not test activation functions such as SoLU, alternative base-model architectures, modern convnets, or the share of polysemantic native neurons.
Whether canonical native-neuron mixtures resolve into a shared feature or related jobs with better tools; the study does not revisit the cited neuron.
Whether the classification of a neuron as polysemantic changes with activation range or explanation-scoring choices.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Multi-modal SAE features at Layers 5, 10, 15, and 20; structured S²AE vs vanilla SAE
reader_labels.reason: Vision and language MS scores and cross-modal consistency rates all rise in the reported paired comparisons (r1–r12); Layer 15 visual cluster alignment also improves (r21). The paper reports EV above 0.99 and fewer active features (r31–r32).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Unimodal SAE feature subsets and regularizer ablations
reader_labels.reason: The pattern is not uniform: vision-only MS falls at Layers 10, 15, and 20, language-only MS falls at Layer 5, and exclusive sparsity alone reduces within-group consistency; the combined regularizers also remain below the no-regularizer group-consistency score (r14–r17, r26, r30).
